title: Industrial Accelerator Act: industry may fail to meet battery demand in EU - electrive.com
content:
The EU is currently debating a draft of the 'Industrial Accelerator Act' (IAA), which aims to boost production and competitiveness within the Union. The ACEA has now presented a study examining whether the European battery supply chain would even be capable of meeting the requirements of this legislative package.
Battery production at VW subsidiary PowerCo in Salzgitter.
Image: PowerCo
The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) commissioned analysts from Mobility Global to conduct a study, which has now resulted in a 19-page executive summary entitled ‘IAA Impact Assessment: European Battery Supply Chain Outlook’. The paper assesses the potential impact on companies in the battery sector and the broader automotive industry if the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) is implemented as proposed by the Commission
in March
. Importantly, the law has not yet been finalised, as negotiations in the European Parliament and Council are still ongoing.
The study’s core message is that stringent localisation requirements for battery production alone are insufficient to guarantee the practical establishment of a battery value chain in Europe. The analysts identify “deeper structural obstacles to localising battery production”, which could take years to overcome.
To break it down: according to the proposed IAA draft, requirements for batteries used in Europe would be introduced in two phases. Six months after the law enters into force (around 2027–2028, according to the study authors), batteries would need to include three EU-sourced components, including battery cells. Three years after adoption (around 2030–2031), this number would increase to five EU-sourced components, including battery cells, battery management systems, and active cathode materials.
Mobility Global examined three scenarios with varying levels of industrial demand for European batteries. The result: in all scenarios, supply cannot keep pace with demand – despite the expected growth of European battery cell production to 306 GWh by 2032. This means that, in the medium term, there will not be enough IAA-compliant batteries to fully supply the electric vehicle industry in the European Union. The study focuses on the next ten years.
ACEA concludes: “Limited supply will remain the key constraint to expanding the number of cars that would be eligible for “made in the EU” incentives. For example, around 3 million cars may be unable to qualify for the associated incentives because of the lack of supply if the IAA enters into force in 2028.” (The so-called “Made in the EU” subsidies are another aspect of the legislative package aimed at ensuring that national programmes primarily subsidise the EU’s own economy.)
ACEA further emphasises that the challenge is even more pronounced for medium- and heavy-duty commercial vehicles than for passenger cars: “The supply-demand gap continues to widen through 2032, reaching 23 GWh, with demand around four times available European supply,” according to a key finding of the study.
The association highlights that the battery value chain in the EU currently has weak structures. The analysts list the following specific issues:
Most planned European gigafactories are focused on NMC batteries, while demand is increasingly shifting towards more cost-effective LFP batteries.
Cells produced in Europe remain significantly more expensive than imported ones.
Announced production capacities are subject to financing, approval, and implementation risks. Announced capacities should therefore not be equated with operational capacities.
Further upstream, Europe continues to face persistent shortages of cathode and anode active materials (CAM/AAM). The analysis suggests that this deficit may only be resolved between 2038 and 2040, even in a low-demand scenario.
ACEA concludes that the results “underline the need for a realistic and economically viable approach to localisation”. The effectiveness of the IAA will ultimately depend not only on the ambition of its requirements but also on “whether Europe can build the upstream capacity, competitive operating conditions and investment framework needed to deliver them in practice”.
The association supplements its assessment with recommendations on how to bridge the gap between ambition and reality. ACEA advises:
Massive upstream investments: To produce CAM and AAM locally and meet demand, substantial investments must be targeted at building foundational upstream components – such as facilities for precursor cathode active material (pCAM) production and graphite purification (AAM).
Shift in policy towards operational support: Policymakers must move beyond merely funding factory construction and begin subsidising ongoing operating costs – particularly high energy costs – while also fast-tracking environmental permits to accelerate project timelines.
Leverage global partnerships and near-shoring: Current EU policy remains highly ambiguous, with unclear “rules of origin” that do not specify whether near-shoring free trade partners like Morocco are treated as equivalent to local EU production. Clarifying these rules to formally include strategic free trade partners is essential; this would enable Europe to avoid high domestic energy costs and utilise international joint ventures to close the material gap.

title: NIO and Geely Enter into Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in Charging and Battery Swapping - Batteries News
content:
NIO and Geely Enter into Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in Charging and Battery Swapping
September 28, 2026, Hangzhou, China – NIO Holding Co., Ltd. (“NIO”) and Zhejiang Geely Holding Group Co., Ltd. (“Geely Holding Group”) entered into a comprehensive strategic cooperation in charging and battery swapping. The two sides have reached broad agreement on cooperation across technology, operations, and capital, and will jointly invest in their charging and battery swapping businesses, share technologies and standards, and develop a shared service network. The partnership marks a new model for open and mutually beneficial cooperation in China’s automotive industry.
Stanley Qu, CFO of NIO and Head of NIO Power, and Ron DAI Qing, Rotating President of Geely Holding Group, exchanged the agreement documents on behalf of the two sides. William Li, Founder, Chairman, and CEO of NIO, Qin Lihong, Co-Founder and President of NIO, Andy AN Conghui, CEO of Geely Holding Group, and Gan Jiayue, CEO of Geely Automobile Group, witnessed the exchange.
Under the agreement, Geely Holding Group will invest in NIO Power through a combination of its 100% equity interest in Yiyi Power, a subsidiary of Geely Holding Group, and RMB 640 million in cash. Upon completion of the transaction, Geely Holding Group will hold a 30% stake in NIO Power. Yiyi Power’s battery swapping business for commercial mobility services will subsequently be integrated into NIO Power. NIO Power will continue to optimize its battery swapping network for commercial fleets, supporting the growth of Yiyi Power’s commercial mobility business. In the meantime, the two sides will co-develop unified battery swapping technologies and standards for consumer-facing vehicle models. Geely Holding Group will develop consumer-facing battery-swappable vehicle models, while NIO Power will provide battery swapping services for these models.
In the smart charging business, NIO will invest in Haohan Energy, a subsidiary of Geely Holding Group. Upon completion of the transaction, NIO will hold a 10% equity stake in Haohan Energy. The two sides will fully connect their charging infrastructure, jointly expanding coverage and improving the operational efficiency of their charging networks.
The deepening partnership between NIO and Geely Holding Group across charging and battery swapping is a concrete step by the two companies to support the goals of the 15th Five-Year Plan for the Development of the Intelligent Connected New Energy Vehicle Industry, address involution-style competition, and improve the allocation of industry resources. It will provide users with a better recharging experience while contributing to China’s green and low-carbon transition.
William Li, Founder,
Chairman, and CEO of NIO, said:
Over the past decade, China’s smart EV industry has made remarkable progress, driven by rapid advances in technology and continued innovation.
”Looking ahead, the industry needs not only to keep innovating, but also to become more efficient at turning innovation into value. This partnership brings together the strengths the two sides have built over the years, with closer collaboration across technology, standards, operations, assets, and capital. It represents an important exploration and innovative step toward addressing involution-style competition and building a more open and mutually beneficial industry ecosystem where automakers can work together to achieve high-quality growth. The collaboration between NIO and Geely in charging and battery swapping is open to the broader industry. We welcome and look forward to more industry peers joining us in creating a better recharging experience for users, supporting the industry’s transition to low-carbon, green energy, and shape a sustainable and brighter future.”
Andy AN Conghui,
CEO of Geely Holding Group, said:
High-quality development of the automotive industry is not about scale alone.
”It calls for more resilient supply chains, higher quality and greater efficiency, safer and greener development, and a more open and collaborative ecosystem. Recharging networks are public infrastructure that serve society as a whole. They should be built together, shared openly, and connected across networks, so that users ultimately benefit the most. Geely Holding Group has long driven innovation in core new energy vehicle technologies, building an all-scenario recharging network that combines charging and swapping. This partnership marks another step toward the high-quality development of China’s intelligent connected new energy vehicle industry. With an open approach and a long-term commitment, Geely Holding Group will work with NIO and other industry partners to build a denser, more reliable, and safer recharging network, making mobility more seamless and worry-free for users.”
As of September 27, 2026, NIO had invested over RMB 20 billion in charging and battery swapping technologies and infrastructure. Its network now comprises 9,433 swapping and charging stations across China, including 4,126 Power Swap Stations and 5,307 charging stations with 30,598 charging piles. NIO has provided more than 220 million charging and battery swapping services, including over 125 million battery swaps and over 99 million charging sessions. With widespread adoption and market validation, battery swapping has become a mainstream recharging solution for new energy vehicles in China. This cooperation will further accelerate the development of NIO’s Power Swap Network. NIO Power aims to have 10,000 Power Swap Stations in operation by 2030, with annual electricity demand across the network expected to exceed 10 billion kWh. As Power Swap Stations become an increasingly important new type of energy infrastructure, their commercial and social value will become more evident.
Geely Holding Group has built an all-scenario recharging ecosystem spanning both charging and swapping. On September 23, 2026, Geely launched its next-generation AI-powered charging technology, ushering in a new era of safe and fast charging driven by AI. Haohan Energy has now deployed 2,500 charging stations with more than 12,000 charging connectors across 232 cities in China, making it one of the industry’s leading charging networks. By the end of 2027, Geely plans to build more than 22,000 charging stations with more than 100,000 charging connectors, including more than 15,000 smart charging stations with over 50,000 smart charging connectors, with the goal of being the first in the industry to achieve full coverage of county-level cities in China. In battery swapping, Yiyi Power is expanding into green and intelligent mobility hubs, automated battery swapping for robotaxis, and smart transportation-energy integration, helping drive innovation across the mobility industry.

title: Samsar Upcycles Electric Vehicle Battery From 1,000th Nissan Leaf - Transforming Old Cars Into New Energy Storage - Batteries News
content:
Samsar Upcycles Electric Vehicle Battery From 1,000th Nissan Leaf – Transforming Old Cars Into New Energy Storage
Samsar has returned over 25 MWh of battery capacity to the field instead of the recycler.
It was a lot of sweat, tears, and late nights. But we got it done and I am so proud of what our team has achieved here in Sugarland. Hitting one-thousand. This is big.”
— CEO Dr. Guillermo Garcia, PhdSUGARLAND, TX, UNITED STATES, September 15, 2026 /
Samsar Resources
, a start-up turned industry leader in the re-manufacturing of electric vehicle
batteries
, is proud to celebrate the transformation of 1,000 Nissan Leaf electric vehicle batteries into new forms of energy storage.
Founded by Steve Hellman, a venture capitalist and founder of Mobility Impact Partners,
was created to capture the full value of lithium batteries by designing batteries made to be remanufactured at the end of their first service life, and by remanufacturing high value lithium batteries like those found in electric vehicles.
For Guillermo Garcia, founding CEO, hitting this milestone was a hard earned moment: “When I joined the team in 2022 we didn’t know if this was going to work. We had this amazing opportunity with Nissan to do something will all the thousands of batteries that were coming out of old Nissan Leafs each year. But every process we developed, every step in building a factory for re-manufacturing EV batteries was new. There was no playbook. It was a lot of sweat, tears, and late nights. But we got it done and I am so proud of what our team has achieved here in Sugarland. Hitting one-thousand. This is big.”
Named after the concept of *samsara*, the cycle of life, death, and rebirth, Samsar designs batteries for a circular economy. Batteries designed to last and designed to be easy to service and repair. Champions of the concept of Design for Remanufacturing (DfRem), by hitting this milestone Samsar has demonstrated that remanufacturing lithium batteries like the Nissan Leaf can be a profitable alternative to recycling or the landfill, while building a more robust US lithium battery supply chain and conserving precious rare earth minerals.
For Kent O’Hara,
former President of Nissan Energy, and new Samsar board member, this moment validates a long standing personal mission:
At Nissan I saw how hungry the world was for energy and knew that in a few years there was going to be millions of EV batteries that would be headed for recycling.
”I knew there must be a way to match the need for power with the growing supply. With this milestone Samsar has proven to be the solution – new energy storage from old cars. It’s affordable, sustainable, and built here, in the USA.”
Samsar Resources remanufactures battery packs from Nissan Leaf sedans at its factory outside of Houston, Texas. Samsar’s cost-conscious approach captures 90% of the value of each pack by downsizing to modules and performing cell-level quality control. Nissan Leaf batteries are the perfect fit for this model thanks to their air-cooled pack architecture and well-understood lifetime performance.
This milestone represents a moment of exponential growth for the company. In 2022 only 20 Nissan packs were re-manufactured. By 2025 over 300 packs a year were being disassembled, tested, and rebuilt, Today, half way through 2026 we proudly announce that we have remanufactured 1,000 Nissan Leaf packs (and counting.)
Battery remanufacturing is the practice of disassembling packs, performing quality control on internal components, and refurbishing as needed. EV batteries are replaced when they reach a threshold of remaining capacity (typically in the range of 80% – 90%).
Industry refers to this threshold as “end-of-life” but that moniker can be deceiving. What it means, really, is that this specific battery is no longer useful for this specific context. It doesn’t mean the battery doesn’t have value.
On the contrary, Nissan Leaf batteries that have left their original vehicles have enormous value. In fact, they are coveted among remanufacturing companies for their air-cooled pack architecture and well-understood lifetime performance. That remaining capacity can be used fruitfully for industries like security, marine, or energy storage at work sites. Samsar uses industry-leading remanufacturing methods to capture that value and sell on to the right customer, at the right price.
Leading the team for this milestone is Carlos Contreras, Operations Manager at Samsar’s Sugarland factory. Carlos is a Manufacturing leader with over 18 years of experience managing operational excellence, quality systems, and EHS compliance across production environments.
Certified as a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt (LSSGB) and Operational Excellence (OpEx-L), he specializes in establishing sustainable systems, optimizing throughput, and building cross-functional teams in high-growth operations.
Carlos has managed manufacturing operations across multiple industrial sectors. Most recently, as a Manufacturing Engineer in piping solutions, he designed technical systems and streamlined production workflows. Previously, he spent nearly four years as a Senior Production Supervisor in fencing manufacturing, directing 65 employees across three departments to meet safety and quality compliance targets. His earlier background includes frontline management, where he managed plant organization, inventory control, and employee training.
The Samsar team needed three years to remanufacture our first 1,000 battery packs. Now that we’ve grown our team and matured our processes, we expect to hit the 2,000 pack milestone sometime in 2027.
You can follow our journey to remanufacturing at scale, and everything else we’re working on, by joining our email list today. Thanks for being part of the adventure!

title: Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium have entered into a joint testing agreement, including a preliminary technology evaluation of ProLogium’s latest Gen4 Superfluidized All Inorganic Solid State Battery Cell Technology - Batteries News
content:
Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium have entered into a joint testing agreement, including a preliminary technology evaluation of ProLogium’s latest Gen4 Superfluidized All Inorganic Solid State Battery Cell Technology
Mercedes-Benz continues to drive solid-state battery technology, and has secured priority access to ProLogium’s latest Gen4 Superfluidized Inorganic Next-Generation Lithium Ceramic Battery (Gen 4 battery) cells.
• ProLogium’s Gen4 battery technology highlights an innovative next generation battery technology approach with balanced and promising characteristics, such as high energy density, cell safety and high rate capability.
• This testing scheme builds upon the nearly 10-year partnership between the two companies that has included Mercedes-Benz’s investing in ProLogium and joint technical development agreements.
TAIPEI, Taiwan – September 24, 2026
– Mercedes-Benz AG and ProLogium Holding Inc. have signed a joint testing agreement, giving Mercedes-Benz priority access to test ProLogium’s latest Gen4 battery cells and further building on the companies’ nearly ten-year partnership in advancing next-generation battery technologies for mobility.
Under the agreement, ProLogium’s Gen4 battery technology will undergo extensive electrical, thermal and safety testing at Mercedes-Benz’s dedicated facilities and specialized external testing institutes. The results will help assess the technology’s suitability for potential use in future vehicles.
The Gen4 battery platform aims to combine five core advantages: intrinsic safety, high performance, high energy density, scalable manufacturing and competitive cost structure. Its safety architecture integrates a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte, ceramic separator technology and ProLogium’s proprietary active safety mechanism, while supporting fast charging, high power output and good low-temperature performance.
Vincent Yang,
Founder and CEO of ProLogium, said:
Over nearly a decade, our collaboration with Mercedes-Benz has evolved from early cell development and validation to testing our latest Gen4 technology for future vehicle applications.
”For next-generation batteries, true value comes from turning years of innovation into scalable manufacturing and commercially viable products. With Mercedes-Benz’s early investment and support for our European expansion, together with the strong support of the French government and the European Union, we are advancing toward large-scale production in Europe and building a manufacturing footprint to serve global markets.”
Jörg Burzer,
Member of the Board of Management, Mercedes‑Benz Group AG, Chief Technology Officer, Development & Procurement, said:
At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility through technological leadership and innovation.
”Our long-standing partnership with ProLogium is a strong example of how we bring the best expertise together to advance next-generation battery technologies. By combining ProLogium’s pioneering solid-state battery approach with Mercedes-Benz’s deep battery development, testing and integration capabilities, we are taking the next step in exploring advanced battery technologies for future electric vehicles.”
Since 2016, the partnership between the two companies has progressed from early hybrid-solid-state GEN 3 which has more than 10 years of commercial references across industries and joint development to potential future vehicle platform planning. Mercedes-Benz became one of ProLogium’s long-term global automotive partners and strategic investors, expanding the relationship beyond product validation. The collaboration has validated multiple lithium ceramic battery formats, including pouch and the first next generation prismatic cells, as well as ProLogium’s Bi-Polar technology.
Mercedes-Benz has a Director on the Board of Directors of ProLogium and is fully supportive of ProLogium’s development plans for its Dunkirk plant as well as ProLogium’s further plans to become publicly listed on the NASDAQ in 4Q2026.
ProLogium’s Taoke Gigafactory in Taiwan has completed GWh-scale manufacturing validation and supports C-sample production, Demo Car programs and future commercial production.
ProLogium’s planned Dunkirk Gigafactory, with a future capacity of up to 44 GWh, is expected to establish localized European manufacturing and supply-chain capacity, replicating the proven production model developed in Taiwan. Once the first phase of this factory is completed, ProLogium will be able to provide commercial cells to European customers at a scale large enough to support electric vehicle platforms on the continent.

title: PowerCo Advances St Thomas Gigafactory with EllisDon Appointment and Phased Development Approach - Batteries News
content:
PowerCo Advances St Thomas Gigafactory with EllisDon Appointment and Phased Development Approach
EllisDon appointed as general contractor as construction advances, with on-site workforce ramping toward ~1,300 at peak
Project progressing through a phased, demand-aligned build, with production ramp-up to scale over time
Major Canadian investment supporting jobs, suppliers, and long-term economic growth across the region
ST. THOMAS, ONTARIO – September 24, 2026 – PowerCo Canada today announced it has selected leading Canadian construction firm EllisDon Corporation as general contractor for its St. Thomas gigafactory, marking a key milestone as the project advances into its next phase of construction.
The appointment enables work on-site to continue building on steady progress since groundbreaking in 2025. Construction is now moving into core infrastructure and structural phases that will support future production.
Joel Karlsberg,
Chief Procurement Officer, PowerCo Canada, said:
Today’s announcement is an important step forward for St. Thomas,
“Partnering with EllisDon allows us to keep construction moving while ensuring we retain the flexibility to scale the facility in line with market demand and long-term industry evolution.”
Initial works are focused on the first phase of development, including core building structures and site-wide infrastructure needed to support future production. Construction includes the production-building shell, mechanical, electrical and plumbing installations, energy and utility systems, and supporting site services. Approximately 60 EllisDon workers are currently on site, expected to ramp up to roughly 1,300 workers at peak, alongside additional personnel supporting parallel project activities.
Max Mantha,
President, Construction, EllisDon, said:
The PowerCo facility represents a transformative investment in Canada’s industrial future, and EllisDon is proud to play a role in its delivery,
“As a Canadian-headquartered, employee-owned company, we are committed to building the infrastructure that will help support Canada’s growing electric vehicle and battery manufacturing sector. This project will create opportunities for skilled tradespeople, local businesses, and communities across southwestern Ontario, and we look forward to working with PowerCo and our partners on this landmark development.”
In parallel, PowerCo is aligning the project’s timeline and product strategy with evolving market demand, technological advancements, and the Volkswagen Group’s long-term strategy. St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029 to accommodate next-generation battery technology, while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve.
Karlsberg
The St. Thomas gigafactory remains a cornerstone of our North American strategy,
“We are continuing to build now while determining how and when the facility scales over time. This is about getting the pacing right—not stepping back—to protect our long-term investment, support regional jobs, and position Canada, Ontario, and St. Thomas to benefit in a dynamic and evolving market.”

title: Hyundai, LG Energy Solution give used EV batteries a second life - Batteries News
content:
Hyundai, LG Energy Solution give used EV batteries a second life
Hyundai Motor Group has joined LG Energy Solution, Hyundai Engineering and Wonik PNE to test an energy storage system that repurposes retired electric vehicle batteries to power fast-charging stations.
The five participating companies — Hyundai Motor, Kia, LG Energy Solution, Hyundai Engineering and Wonik PNE — launched the pilot Thursday at Wonik PNE’s facility in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province.
Hyundai Motor Group described it as Korea’s first project directly linking used batteries from Hyundai and Kia electric vehicles to EV fast-charging infrastructure.
The demonstration facility features a 200-kilowatt-hour used-battery energy storage system, or UBESS, built with battery packs recovered from EVs based on the group’s Electric-Global Modular Platform.
The system stores electricity during off-peak hours, when rates are lower, and supplies it to fast chargers during periods of high demand. The approach is intended to reduce pressure on the power grid, lower charging costs and extend the life of EV batteries.
Hyundai Motor and Kia will lead technical verification and develop potential business models. LG Energy Solution will manufacture the UBESS using the recovered battery packs and assess its performance and safety through the company’s battery diagnostic and management technologies.
Hyundai Engineering will evaluate the system’s commercial viability and integration with EV charging infrastructure, while Wonik PNE will oversee equipment operation and technical testing.
The partners will test charging and discharging control algorithms, system safety and reliability, battery performance and charging-service quality under real-world operating conditions.

title: As the EU Digital Battery Passport Deadline Nears, Carbmee Argues the Real Test Is Data, Not the QR Code - Batteries News
content:
As the EU Digital Battery Passport Deadline Nears, Carbmee Argues the Real Test Is Data, Not the QR Code
With the 18 February 2027 deadline approaching, Carbmee’s leadership makes the case that battery passport readiness is a strategic data capability, not a last-minute compliance exercise.
BERLIN — From 18 February 2027, electric vehicles, light means of transport, and industrial batteries above 2 kWh cannot be placed on the EU market without a Digital Battery Passport under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542. carbmee, the environmental intelligence company, is urging manufacturers to treat the requirement as an operational milestone that demands preparation now, not a documentation task that can wait for the deadline.
The company’s central argument is that the visible part of the regulation, the QR code on the battery, is the least important part. Behind it sit roughly 80 required data fields, tiered access rights for the public, regulators, and supply chain actors, verified documentation, carbon calculations, recycled-content evidence, and a complete audit trail that must stay current across a battery’s life.
“The QR code is the door. The question every board should be asking is whether there is anything credible behind it,” said
Christian Heinrich
, Co-Founder and CEO, Carbmee. “Battery passport readiness is not a legal formality. It is a test of whether a company can produce verified, product-level data on demand, and the companies treating it that way now will hold an advantage over those still assembling spreadsheets in 2027.”
Carbmee notes that several obligations are already active ahead of the headline deadline. The EU Batteries Regulation has applied since 18 February 2024, and EV carbon footprint declarations have been required since February 2025. Companies without granular data default to proxy values and carry higher assumed emissions, turning a data gap into a direct cost.
The company also highlights that responsibility is legally concentrated on the operator placing the battery on the market, while the underlying data is distributed across raw material suppliers, component makers, battery producers, OEMs, and recyclers. That mismatch, carbmee argues, is why battery passport readiness is a governance question spanning compliance, sustainability, engineering, procurement, IT, operations, and legal, and cannot be solved by any single team.

Its platform, carbmee EIS™, manages 5.8 Gt CO2e and is trusted by leading enterprises including Maersk, ZEISS, ZF, Heraeus, and KWS.

SES AI’s Chungju Battery Facility Achieves ISO 9001:2015 Certification for Production of NDAA-Compliant Drone Cells
Certification strengthens SES AI’s quality and manufacturing infrastructure as the Company scales production and remains on track to reach approximately one million cells of annual production capacity
WOBURN, Mass.–(
BUSINESS WIRE
SES AI Corporation
(“SES AI”) (NYSE: SES), a global leader in the development and manufacturing of AI-enhanced high-performance Li-Metal and Li-ion batteries, today announced that its battery manufacturing facility in Chungju, South Korea has achieved ISO 9001:2015 certification for its quality management system. The certification was issued by the Korea ESG Certification Body following an independent assessment of the facility’s quality management processes. SES AI also announced that recent changes by the South Korean government to export control standards on energy density for secondary batteries provide significant competitive advantages for the export of SES AI NDAA-compliant pouch cells.
Qichao Hu,
Founder and CEO of SES AI, said:
Achieving ISO 9001:2015 certification is an important milestone as we scale our drone battery business,
“Drone customers need not only high energy and power density, but also manufacturing quality, traceability, consistency and a dependable supply chain. Our Chungju facility brings these capabilities together and strengthens our ability to supply NDAA-compliant pouch cells manufactured in Korea to customers in the United States and other markets.”
SES AI has been expanding its Chungju manufacturing operation in response to growing demand for high-performance batteries for drones and other advanced mobility applications. The Company has recently completed the scale up to an annual production capacity of approximately one million Li-Metal and Li-ion pouch cells, representing a significant expansion of SES AI’s manufacturing capability for drone and other high-performance battery applications. The Chungju facility manufactures high-energy and high-power density Li-Metal and Li-ion pouch cells for drone applications, including NDAA-compliant cells designed to serve customers requiring secure and dependable battery supply chains.
Earlier this month, the South Korean government raised export control energy density threshold for secondary batteries to 500Wh/kg, while the majority of other countries continue to use the old 350Wh/kg threshold, making trading logistics and compliance even more favorable for Korea-produced cells. Additional comments from SES AI on this recent announcement and its array of high-energy and high-power density pouch cells can be found on its
LinkedIn page.
Battery manufacturing for drones is rapidly moving from small-volume specialty production toward a scaled industrial supply chain,
“With ISO 9001 certification, NDAA-compliant sourcing, easier export compliance, manufacturing in Korea and our expansion toward approximately one million cells of annual production capacity, we are building the foundation to serve growing demand from the global drone industry.”
SES AI’s drone cells combine high energy density and high-power density with the Company’s battery material, cell engineering and manufacturing capabilities. The Company is developing both Li-Metal and advanced Li-ion pouch cells for demanding drone missions where flight time, payload, power and battery weight are critical performance requirements.
The scope of the ISO 9001:2015 certification SES AI received is “manufacture of storage batteries, and research and development of batteries and battery materials.” The certification further strengthens the manufacturing infrastructure supporting this expansion and establishes a standardized quality management framework across processes including incoming material control, cell manufacturing, inspection, testing, traceability, corrective actions and continuous improvement.
ISO 9001:2015 is an internationally recognized quality management standard focused on consistent processes, product quality, customer requirements, risk management and continuous improvement. The certification followed an independent audit by the Korea ESG Certification Body covering the manufacture of storage batteries and the research and development of batteries and battery materials.

title: Volkswagen Group, PowerCo and Gotion deepen strategic partnership - Batteries News
content:
Volkswagen Group, PowerCo and Gotion deepen strategic partnership
The companies are expanding their long-standing strategic partnership to include the industrial production of LFP battery cells and cathode active materials.
Accelerated development of a regional battery supply chain for Europe through the establishment of joint ventures at the Valencia (Spain), Šurany (Slovak Republic) and Kenitra (Morocco) sites.
Valencia to be developed into European production hub for LFP batteries.
Thomas Schmall: “Gotion has been a close partner of the Volkswagen Group for many years. We are now expanding our partnership into joint industrial production of LFP batteries to strengthen Europe’s battery industry. This marks a major breakthrough for both companies.”
Salzgitter/Hefei/Valencia. Volkswagen Group, PowerCo SE and Gotion High-tech have agreed to deepen their strategic partnership and jointly accelerate the development of a regional battery supply chain for Europe. Building on their cooperation since 2020, the partners agreed on establishing three joint ventures at the Valencia (Spain), Šurany (Slovak Republic) and Kenitra (Morocco) sites for the industrial production of LFP battery cells and cathode material. The agreement also covers joint procurement and sales activities in Europe. Separately, Volkswagen Group has announced that it has entered into definitive agreements to sell 5.3 % equity stake in Gotion to optimize equity structures and support long-term strategic synergies. Upon completion of the transaction, Volkswagen will continue to hold a significant stake in Gotion.
LFP batteries offer competitive costs, a long service life and high levels of robustness, making them a key technology for affordable electric mobility in the volume segment. Demand in Europe is expected to grow strongly in the coming years: According to forecasts, LFP’s market share could rise from around 10 percent today to between 40 and 60 percent by 2030. At the same time, Europe currently has no relevant LFP battery production capacity.
The partnership with Gotion strengthens Europe’s position in the global LFP battery market. Together, the partners will expand regional LFP battery production, diversify sources of supply for key cathode active materials, and thereby strengthen supply security and the competitiveness of the European battery industry.
Thomas Schmall,
Member of the Board of Management of Volkswagen Group for Technology and Chairman of the Supervisory Board of PowerCo SE:
I am delighted that we are expanding our long-standing partnership with Gotion into the joint industrial production of LFP batteries to strengthen Europe’s battery industry.
”This marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings us one step closer to the forefront of electric mobility. Volkswagen is the first European automotive manufacturer to cover the entire battery value chain, from development and cathode materials through to production.”
Li Zhen,
Chairman of Gotion Hith-tech, said:
Six years of close collaboration between Volkswagen and Gotion have built deep mutual trust and a relationship that empowers both sides—one that has long since moved beyond ordinary business to become a partnership bound by a shared future.
”Today, together with Volkswagen Group and PowerCo, we are accelerating our global strategic cooperation. Through cross-shareholdings and three joint sites, we are anchoring our shared strategy to localise battery production in Europe, racing to seize the opportunities of global electric mobility, and jointly forging a new paradigm of world-class, win-win cooperation in the lithium battery industry.”
Frank Blome,
CEO of PowerCo SE, said:
Volkswagen and PowerCo are building Europe’s battery industry.
”The partnership with Gotion is the next milestone on this path: It strengthens the resilience of our value chain, accelerates industrialization and combines PowerCo’s capabilities with the strengths of a long-standing partner.”
Diversifying the battery supply chain
Volkswagen Group, PowerCo and Gotion have been working closely and successfully together since 2020. Gotion is both a cell supplier to the Volkswagen Group and a strategic partner of PowerCo.
With the new joint ventures, the partners are strategically expanding this proven cooperation into the industrial production of LFP battery cells and cathode active material. Across the three sites, they will also share investments and industrial responsibilities. The agreement therefore supports Volkswagen Group’s long-term plans to establish a European battery supply chain and strengthens PowerCo’s growth plan.
Valencia / Spain: LFP battery cells
The PowerCo gigafactory currently under construction in Valencia is envisaged to be transferred to a joint venture. The agreement provides for PowerCo to hold a 51 percent stake in the joint venture and to remain the majority shareholder. The joint venture is intended to be jointly managed by PowerCo and Gotion. One major goal is to develop the site into a European production hub for Unified Cells based on LFP technology. The planned investments and job creation measures remain as announced.
Šurany / Slovak Republic: LFP battery cells
The Gotion cell factory in Šurany is intended to be transferred to a joint venture. The agreement provides for Gotion to hold a 51 percent stake in the joint venture and to remain the majority shareholder. The joint venture is intended to be jointly managed by PowerCo and Gotion, with a focus on LFP cells for both EV applications and energy storage systems (ESS).
Kenitra / Morocco: LFP cathode material
The joint venture in Kenitra is planning to establish a new production facility to produce cathode material for LFP batteries. The facility is intended to contribute to the diversification of sources of supply for key cathode active materials, increase supply security and expand the regional value chain. Gotion will hold a 51 percent stake and be the majority shareholder of the joint venture. PowerCo and Gotion will manage the joint venture together.
Financial details
Under the terms of the agreement, PowerCo is expected to contribute in total around EUR 470 million to the Šurany and Kenitra sites by 2030 to acquire its 49 % stake. In return, the agreement provides for Gotion to invest around EUR 1.1 billion to acquire its 49 % stake in the Valencia site, reflecting the scale and strategic importance of the European production hub. The agreement remains subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions, including approval by the Gotion shareholders’ meeting.
Furthermore, building on the long-standing partnership, and with the view to optimizing shareholding structures and supporting long-term strategic synergy, Volkswagen Group, through its subsidiary Volkswagen (China) Investment Co., Ltd. (VCIC), has entered into definitive agreements to sell 5.3 % equity stake in Gotion. As Volkswagen had previously agreed not to exercise voting rights for part of its shareholding, the targeted transaction will not reduce the voting rights in Gotion exercised by Volkswagen Group. Volkswagen Group’s Board of Directors representation in Gotion and other nomination rights remain unaffected by the targeted transaction. Following completion of the transaction, Volkswagen will continue to be engaged as a strategic investor in Gotion. The transaction is subject to all required regulatory clearances.

South 8 Begins Volume Production of Extreme Cold Weather Lithium-Ion Batteries for Defense Customers
Since executing a $9.2 million PowerForward Battery Manufacturing Grant agreement earlier this year, South 8 has scaled manufacturing of LiGas enabled lithium-ion battery cells in San Diego, California
SAN DIEGO–(
BUSINESS WIRE
)–South 8 Technologies’ new semi-automated battery cell manufacturing line is now operational, marking a significant milestone in growing US domestic cell manufacturing capacity. The line will support 5 MWh of annual cylindrical cell production in 2027, enhancing South 8’s ability to serve defense and specialty markets requiring reliable battery performance in extreme cold.
The manufacturing expansion supports production of South 8’s ARCTIC™ AE35 18650 cell, which uses a proprietary LiGas liquefied gas electrolyte to enable reliable charge and discharge from −60 °C to +60 °C (−76 °F to +140 °F).
The new manufacturing line will produce cells for defense customers, including 3ME Technology and Galvion. Both are commercializing LiGas enabled battery solutions for demanding defense and cold weather applications, creating a clear path from qualification to production as South 8 scales cell production capacity through 2027.
In parallel with the production buildout, South 8 has established supplier agreements for key cell materials and components to develop a resilient supply chain that avoids reliance on foreign entities of concern (FEOCs). Both the cells and the proprietary LiGas electrolyte will be produced at South 8’s San Diego facility, providing customers with a domestically manufactured battery cell and a defined pathway toward meeting applicable National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) sourcing requirements once those rules are finalized.
Rusty Heffner,
Vice President of Strategy at South 8 Technologies, said:
Customers need battery cells that perform in extreme environments while also reducing supply chain risk,
“South 8 is scaling production of the AE35 cell to address both needs. We provide the cold weather performance our customers require while building cells domestically with a supply chain that was selected to comply with the NDAA Section 842 rules. We enhance the capability of our customers’ products and give them confidence that they will have a reliable domestic source of battery cells that meets emerging DOW regulations.”
These capabilities are increasingly important for defense and specialty cold weather applications, where both battery performance and supply chain security can be critical. South 8 customers build packs and platforms for applications including unmanned systems, communications equipment, remote sensing, soldier power, and other equipment expected to operate reliably in extreme environments.

title: Closing the White Space Gap in Global Supply Chains
content:
Closing the White Space Gap in Global Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Infios is working to close the gap between AI adoption. Credit: Infios
The biggest gap in supply chain technology right now is not at the top of the market or among smaller businesses, but the middle
If you run supply chain execution for a business between US$100m and US$2.5bn in revenue, you know the squeeze. You are carrying enterprise-grade complexity — multiple regions, multiple systems, constant disruption — without an enterprise-sized team or budget to absorb it. You earned that complexity one reasonable decision at a time: a new channel here, a new geography there, B2B and B2C running side by side. Each made sense on its own. Together, they built an operation that looks like a Tier 1 enterprise, but often still runs on a tech stack built for a smaller, simpler company.
That is the white space in supply chain technology: companies large enough to face
enterprise-level execution complexity
, but often underserved by tools built for either the largest enterprises or much smaller businesses. Software gets designed for one end of the revenue spectrum or the other. The middle inherits what is left over.
The gap is not in your planning, but in your execution
Most of the time, you already know something changed. You have the forecast, the alert, the dashboard telling you a shipment is late or a site is short on labor. Detection usually is not the problem. The problem is what happens next: getting from that signal to a coordinated response across execution domains that do not naturally share context.
Orders, warehouse and transportation each run as their own world, with their own data and their own logic. When a carrier slips, it is not only a transportation problem. It is a warehouse labor problem, an inventory problem and a customer-promise problem at the same time. But the signal does not cross those domains on its own. Someone has to carry it by hand: pulling data out of one system and into another, working the phones and deciding who owns the trade off.
That coordination is where the time goes, and where the cost lands.
Supply chains rarely break in planning
. They break in execution: in the handoffs between systems that were never designed to talk to each other. The delay is not that no one saw the disruption. It is how long it takes to coordinate a response across those execution domains and act before it reaches a customer.
Omar Akilah, Senior Vice President, Product & Industry Strategy at Infios
Enterprise complexity, without enterprise resources
Large enterprises absorb those gaps with money and people. They have dedicated teams whose entire job is stitching systems together. In the mid-market, that team often does not exist. What
fills the gap instead
is workaround after workaround: another point solution, a third-party integrator bridging the OMS and ERP, an analyst reconciling numbers across systems that should reconcile themselves. Each fix looks reasonable on its own. Stacked together, they become the problem. The bill arrives quietly through licensing, integration upkeep, manual labor, error rates and decisions made a day too late. The margin you were trying to protect erodes as you grow. Complexity scales, but the cost of managing it scales faster.
The industry is starting to put a number on the gap between the moment a signal changes and the moment the business acts on it. In a 2026 study, Incisiv quantified it at more than five cents on every dollar of revenue, an estimated US$55m a year for a US$1bn business. But you do not need a study to recognise the cost. You have lived it every time a promise that looked safe at 9:00am was gone by lunch.
Infios aims to connect orders across one system. Credit: Infios
What AI actually changes here
For years, coordinated execution across orders, warehouse and transportation was something you could only get by building it yourself, the way Tier 1 enterprises did: with custom integrations and the teams to run them. That is what kept it out of reach for the middle. AI changes the economics of that.
Here is the distinction that matters: AI does not eliminate the need for coordinated execution. It makes coordinated execution more valuable.
First, orders, warehouse and transportation have to work from a shared execution foundation, so data and action are available across the business instead of trapped inside each system. That foundation is real work, and AI does not replace it.
Second, AI changes how the business uses that foundation. It can interpret signals, assemble context across domains, recommend or decide on a response, and orchestrate action within the rules the business has set. The expensive part was rarely the insight alone. It was the manual reconciliation and orchestration in between, and that is the part AI can take on.
That shift has a name: Intelligent Supply Chain Execution. Instead of three execution domains that transact in isolation and reconcile after the fact, orders, warehouse and transportation operate as one coordinated model: sensing a change, deciding on a response, acting across the connected systems, and learning from the outcome, all within the boundaries the business defines. It extends the systems already in place rather than replacing them.
That matters because mid-market leaders do not need to jump straight from manual coordination to full autonomy. Trust in AI is being earned in stages, and the market is moving that way on purpose. In Relex's State of Supply Chain 2026, 67% of leaders say they have grown more confident in AI over the past year, and just 3% report a decline; only about 10% trust it to make a critical decision without a human reviewing it first. Leaders trust AI to inform a decision well before they trust it to make one, and that is exactly the right instinct.
How it works in practice
For mid-market companies, the practical path is not to replace every system. It is to connect the execution workflows that create the most friction and apply intelligence where coordination breaks down.
That is the problem Infios is working to solve. Infios AI powers Intelligent Supply Chain Execution by helping teams sense what is happening across the supply chain, decide the best course of action, act faster and learn from the outcome. Infios Archer is the agentic execution system that turns that intelligence into coordinated decisions and action, using AI
agents that operate
within defined guardrails, inside and across supply chain workflows.
Autonomy is earned, not assumed. You extend it the same way you would with a new hire. It moves in stages: first, agents that recommend an action with a clear rationale; then agents that execute within policies your team has already defined; and eventually, once the trust is there, agents that run a workflow end to end inside guardrails.
You do not hand over the operation on day one. Start with your highest-friction workflow, such as transportation exceptions or order changes, prove the value there and expand from it.
The model is not theoretical. In production, one global apparel brand cut order release from eight hours to eight minutes; a US online retailer reduced backorders by 70%; a logistics provider reached an 83% autonomy rate on automated order entry. In each case, the systems were not replaced. They were made to work as one.
There is a new execution model. Credit: Infios
Coordinated execution becomes the advantage
The next few years will separate the companies that
coordinate execution from the ones
that keep managing around the gap.
The businesses that pull ahead will be the ones that can sense change as it happens, coordinate a response across their systems in real time, and protect both the customer promise and the margin while conditions keep moving. The ones that do not will keep buying workarounds and keep paying for complexity through manual coordination, slower decisions and margin erosion.
Closing the white space gap will not be about adding more software. It will be about making the systems you already run act as one, so the technology finally follows the strategy instead of setting its limits.
About the author
Omar Akilah is SVP, Product & Industry Strategy at Infios, where he helps shape product direction and industry strategy across the company’s supply chain execution portfolio. A proven transformational leader, Omar brings a deep understanding of how  technology, operations and evolving industry needs intersect, and how organisations can apply the principles of Intelligent Supply Chain Execution to turn complexity into business advantage.
Throughout his career, Omar has led innovation across inventory visibility, omnichannel fulfillment, buy-online/pick-up-in-store, ship-from-store, last- mile delivery and operational execution to promise. He has a unique ability to translate tactical challenges into strategic opportunities, identify areas for re-engineering and align cross-functional teams, around scalable capabilities that deliver meaningful customer and business value.
Omar has worked at leading brands, including Apple, Target, Ingram Micro and Yantriks. His expertise spans Product Management, eCommerce, Direct-to-Consumer innovation, Last Mile strategy, global logistics, omnichannel fulfillment, last-mile strategy and 3PL integration. He also has deep experience in OMS, WMS, and TMS and ERP implementations. A strategic and collaborative leader, Omar brings together customer insight, industry expertise and technology strategy to help organizations improve execution focus across retail, logistics, and the broader supply chain ecosystem to prepare them for what comes next.

packaging company
, to trace the origin and movement of European Union Deforestation Regulation of relevant materials across its Europe, Middle East and Africa supply chain.
The programme covers more than 250 plants and facilities in more than 30 countries.
Together, Accenture and osapiens aim to give DS Smith clear, auditable proof of where the materials in its
packaging come from
, ahead of the regulation's enforcement.
Matias Pollmann-Larsen, Global Risk, Resilience and Sustainable Value Chain lead at Accenture, says: “What DS Smith has done with Accenture and osapiens is build the data foundation needed to stay ahead of these challenges, rather than simply responding to the next regulation when it arrives.”
Key facts: DS Smith's EUDR Programme
Accenture and osapiens have partnered with DS Smith to trace EUDR-relevant materials across its supply chain
The programme spans more than 250 plants and facilities in over 30 countries
Nearly 25,000 supply chain workflows are now managed through the osapiens HUB platform
Suppliers are onboarded digitally, with compliance data managed through one centralised system
Wood fibre, DS Smith's principal material, falls within EUDR's scope alongside commodities like cocoa and palm oil
Matias Pollmann-Larsen, Global Risk, Resilience and Sustainable Value Chain lead at Accenture. Credit: Content Publishing
Inside DS Smith's EUDR traceability programme
DS Smith, Accenture and osapiens
reviewed sourcing
, manufacturing, logistics and sales processes across the company's EMEA operations.
Sakis Miliotis, IT director for Paper, Paper Supply Chain, Recycling and Sustainability at DS Smith, says: “Working with Accenture and osapiens, we have built something that works at scale.”
Accenture drove process transformation, supplier enablement, systems integration and programme scaling, while osapiens supplied the technology platform behind the initiative.
Previously separate supply chain systems, onboarding and reporting processes were consolidated onto a single platform, the osapiens HUB.
Nearly 25,000 supply chain workflows are now managed through the osapiens HUB platform.
Suppliers are onboarded digitally, with traceability and
compliance data managed
through one centralised system.
The company can trace EUDR-relevant materials from origin through production and distribution.
The work establishes a foundation for DS Smith to meet future sustainability and product compliance requirements beyond EUDR itself.
Working with Accenture and osapiens, we have built something that works at scale
Sakis Miliotis, IT director for Paper, Paper Supply Chain, Recycling and Sustainability at DS Smith
Deforestation rules and compliance
Under the EU Deforestation Regulation, large and medium operators and traders must comply from 30 December 2026, with most smaller enterprises given until 30 June 2027.
The rules require a Due Diligence Statement for every product batch, submitted through the EU's TRACES system.
Each batch must include GPS-verified geolocation of all plots, supplier documentation and a deforestation
risk assessment
“Nearly 80% of supply chain leaders tell us that uncertain geopolitical regulatory requirements have made operating their businesses more difficult over the past six months. That pressure is not going away,” says Matias.
Meeting these requirements is a key focus for businesses, as non-compliance carries a minimum fine of 4% of a company's annual EU turnover.
Operators sourcing from higher-risk countries face stricter punishments, with authorities required to inspect at least 9% of relevant operators by volume in those cases.
According to Kolvita, around 30% of upstream actors currently have
traceability systems
in place capable of meeting the regulation's plot-level requirements.
Incomplete or inaccurate geolocation data is one of the most common reasons for the rejection of due diligence statements.
DS Smith's own commodity exposure, principally wood fibre for its packaging, sits squarely within EUDR's scope, alongside cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rubber, soya and cattle.

title: M&S and New Look Partner for Circular Textile Value Chains
content:
M&S and New Look Partner for Circular Textile Value Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Leading brands are collaborating to bring greater resilience and sustainability to textile value chains. Credit: Wokephoto17
Lynda Petherick, CEO at New Look, explores how The Circuit is a collaborative opportunity to bring resilience and sustainability to UK textile value chains
The UK fashion and textile industry contributes £62bn (US$82.15bn) to the UK economy, according to Oxford Economics and the UK Fashion and Textile Association (UKFT).
According to the report, it supports 1.3 million jobs and is one of the largest sectors in the country.
However, the industry also has a major environmental impact, which is why some of the major UK retailers are teaming up to
launch a collaborative model designed
to bring greater circularity into the UK’s fashion industry.
An industry concern
As the fashion industry falls under increasing levels of scrutiny for its emissions and global impact, organisations around the world are working to integrate initiatives or collaborative efforts to minimise their impact.
In the UK, approximately 1.4 million tonnes of post-consumer textiles were generated in 2024. Out of this, almost half is non-reusable. This demonstrates a need for greater investment in the infrastructure which can recover, reuse and recycle textile resources.
Consumers are beginning to turn more towards
second-hand clothing items
, rather than buying at full price from the retailer. Circularity is becoming more of a priority for consumers and businesses alike, as it is seen as a more sustainable way of purchasing, as well as a more cost-efficient format.
To transform how waste is managed in the UK, five companies are teaming up to generate new life in fashion.
New Look, M&S, Sainsbury’s and Oxfam have partnered with Circle-8, announcing the launch of The Circuit. This is a new collaborative model, designed to bring together retailers, textile recovery partners, automated sorting, recyclers, digital innovators and manufacturers. The aim is to transform the UK’s generated post-consumer textiles into future circular raw materials, building new circular textile value chains.
“If we want circularity to become a meaningful part of the fashion industry, we need to move beyond ambition and start building the infrastructure and partnerships that can make it work,” Lynda Petherick, CEO at New Look, explains to Supply Chain Digital.
Lynda Petherick, CEO at New Look
“The Circuit partnership is an opportunity to make this work in practice, bringing different parts of the industry together to find new uses for textiles that might
otherwise go to waste
. For New Look, being involved means learning now, and helping to shape solutions that can work at scale, and building greater resilience into our supply chain for the future.”
Textile waste numbers
Every year, the UK discards around 336,000 tonnes of clothing every year (WRAP)
Approximately, 100 billion clothing items are made each year (McKinsey)
The fashion industry contributes an estimated 10% of global carbon emissions (UNEP)
Approximately 92 million tonnes of waste come from the fashion industry every year (UNEP)
Less than 1% of all textiles are recycled around the world (European Parliament)
Developing innovative pathways
Due to the increasing number of synthetic materials being used in clothing, much of it cannot be recycled or re-used. As a result, the initiative is looking to
transform the potential of these waste textiles
and develop them into something new. The first phase of the collaboration will be testing, learning and developing what is needed in order to create operations that can be scaled.
New solutions are needed to recover and recycle these materials, as the systems needed for post-consumer textiles are still emerging.
"The Circuit is an important step forward, bringing together organisations from across the retail industry to help create viable routes for non-reusable textiles and support a more circular future for fashion,” explains Katharine Beacham, Head of Sustainability & Materials in Fashion, Home & Beauty at M&S.
Katharine Beacham, Head of Sustainability & Materials in Fashion, Home & Beauty at M&S
The Circuit is designed to develop new pathways into this recovery process, looking to sort and pre-process discarded textiles. These can be on a small scale, but the collaborative initiative is aiming to develop this significantly.
With large brands involved, alongside companies across the value chain – such as manufacturers, second-hand retailers and recyclers – The Circuit is working towards consistency, scale and supported commercial conditions which can accelerate textile recycling viability.
Ben Smith, Managing Director of Sainsbury's Tu Clothing, adds, "Creating a more circular future for textiles will take collaboration and innovation across the whole industry. The Circuit is an exciting opportunity to work alongside partners from across the value chain to explore how post-consumer textiles generated here in the UK can be given a new life as
valuable raw materials
Ben Smith, Managing Director at Sainsbury's TU
Integrating circularity
Fashion value chains are undergoing a period of transformation, and this initiative will guide it towards a positive one. As more consumers are buying second-hand or thinking more consciously about where their clothing comes from, this responsible process enables buyers to have new clothes with the environmental responsibility of old ones.
The UK economy will see significant benefit from this initiative, as there will be greater job creation and manufacturing opportunities. Alongside this, there will be automated sorting and pre-processing. This will take place close to where the textiles are generated, therefore turning it into feedstock for regional and global supply chains.
Through this initiative, there will be a development of mechanical and chemical recycling processes, which will transform post-consumer textiles into raw materials. This then allows even more innovative production to take place, as manufacturers will have a clean slate for production.
The materials will have increased routes to markets and there will be a heightened number of products from recovered materials.
Rachel Cosgrove-Pearce, Retail Director at Oxfam, explains, “Developing the infrastructure to recover valuable fibres from end-of-use textiles is an important part of building a fashion system that uses fewer virgin resources and creates less environmental harm, and The Circuit brings together the expertise and investment needed to move this forward at scale.”
Rachel Cosgrove-Pearce, Retail Director at Oxfam
Circle-8 is developing the infrastructure, partnerships and commercial frameworks for the initiative, driving a connected network for the project. It is working to connect post-consumer textile recovery with future circular material supply, meaning there will be a feedstock for existing and emerging textile recyclers.
“The retailers who help build circular textile value chains today will be best positioned to influence and benefit from them tomorrow,” adds Cyndi Rhoades, CEO and Co-Founder of Circle-8 Textile Ecosystems.
Cyndi Rhoades, CEO and Co-Founder of Circle-8 Textile Ecosystems
“Through The Circuit, we’re powering the relationships, infrastructure and commercial frameworks needed to make that possible. No one organisation can create a
circular textile value chain
alone, and we look forward to welcoming others to The Circuit.”
The first phase is set to begin in January 2027, with an initial focus on automated textile sorting. It will also develop a framework for traceability reporting, alongside the ability to identify opportunities, new relationships and scalable operational models.
If we want circularity to become a meaningful part of the fashion industry, we need to move beyond ambition and start building the infrastructure and partnerships that can make it work.
Lynda Petherick, CEO at New Look
Key companies
New Look
CEO: Lynda Petherick
HQ: Dorset, UK
New Look is a British fast-fashion retailer founded in 1969, targeting young women and men with trend-led, affordable clothing. Operating both physical stores and online, the brand has faced financial challenges in recent years, undergoing restructuring and store closures. Known for accessible prices and quick trend turnaround, New Look competes with brands like H&M and Zara in the value fashion segment.
CEO: Stuart Machin
HQ: London, UK
Marks & Spencer is an iconic British retailer established in 1884, offering clothing, home products, and food. Their clothing ranges span womenswear, menswear, and children's wear, positioned at mid-market pricing with emphasis on quality and classic styling. M&S has invested heavily in sustainability initiatives, including Plan A commitments, and maintains strong brand recognition despite facing competition from both value and premium retailers.
Sainsbury’s
CEO: Simon Roberts
HQ: London, UK
TU is Sainsbury's in-house clothing brand, launched in 2004, offering affordable fashion for the whole family. Available in larger Sainsbury's supermarkets and online, TU provides convenient, budget-friendly options competing with Tesco's F&F and ASDA's George. The brand focuses on essential wardrobe pieces, seasonal trends, and school uniforms, capitalizing on grocery shopping footfall to drive clothing sales alongside weekly shopping trips.
CEO: Richard Hawkes
HQ: Oxford, UK
Oxfam is an international charity operating secondhand shops selling donated clothing, books, and goods to fund poverty relief and humanitarian work. Their stores promote sustainable fashion through clothing reuse and have become increasingly fashionable destinations for vintage and pre-loved items. Oxfam has launched initiatives like Oxfam Online Shop and fashion campaigns highlighting environmental impacts of fast fashion, positioning charity retail as ethical consumption.
Circle-8 Textile Ecosystems
CEO: Cyndi Rhoades
HQ: London, UK
Circle-8 Textile Ecosystems is an innovative company addressing textile waste through circular economy solutions. They collect post-consumer textiles and transform them into new materials and products, diverting waste from landfills. Using advanced sorting and recycling technologies, Circle-8 works with brands and municipalities to create closed-loop systems where textiles are continuously recycled, supporting fashion industry sustainability goals and reducing environmental impact.

DHL: Agentic AI Reshapes Supply Chains and Workforce
Prioritise Us

Katja Busch, Chief Commercial Officer at DHL, says Agentic AI is reshaping supply chains as automation and human expertise increasingly converge
DHL has released the eighth edition of its biennial flagship research report, the Logistics Trend Radar 8.0, revealing how artificial intelligence,
robotics and physical automation
are changing supply chain operations.
The report analyses how companies are shifting from simple digital assistance toward full operational autonomy.
“Supply chains are changing faster than ever as AI and workforce trends increasingly influence one another. The organisations that succeed will be those that understand these shifts early and are able to turn them into practical advantages for their business and their people,” says Katja Busch, Chief Commercial Officer at DHL and Head of DHL Customer Solutions & Innovation.
Katja Busch, Chief Commercial Officer at DHL. Credit: Katja Busch via LinkedIn
DHL's Logistics Trend Radar
DHL’s eighth edition of its biennial Logistics Trend Radar
Agentic AI, AI Commerce, Compute Economy and Humanoids are added as new trends
The report highlights AI's shift from digital assistance to autonomous action
Employee Belonging and the Augmented Workplace emerge as key workforce trends
DHL Group generated approximately €82.9bn (US$94.2bn) in revenue in 2025
Autonomous AI and workforce augmentation
Developed by DHL Customer Solutions & Innovation, the Logistics Trend Radar 8.0 maps key technological, business and social trends shaping global trade over the next decade.
A core breakthrough highlighted in the report is the evolution of
Agentic AI
Unlike earlier generative tools or static dashboards that merely respond to prompts or summarise historical data, Agentic AI operates autonomously toward predefined goals.
According to Gartner, by 2028 more than 70% of enterprise supply chain organisations will adopt physical AI, collaborative robotics and multi-client automated storage and retrieval
systems to address labour
shortages and maximise warehouse efficiency.
Working alongside AI Analytics, these systems uncover deep operational patterns to predict disruptions, forecast demand and recommend real-time actions at scale.
This software intelligence works directly with physical automation to reshape frontline operations.
DHL’s analysis reveals that technology, such as wearable sensors, remote equipment operation, collaborative robotics and AI-powered workplace assistants are creating a safer, augmented workspace.
People remain the driving force behind every successful supply chain
Thomas Ogilvie, Chief Human Resources Officer and Labour Director, DHL Group.
Human and robotics partnership
The transition from passive digital assistance to autonomous decision-making marks a pivotal evolution
across global distribution networks
One of the most significant findings of the Logistics Trend Radar 8.0 is the emergence of Agentic AI, identified as one of the report's most impactful trends.
DHL says Agentic AI can autonomously plan, decide and act toward defined goals, enabling “closer collaboration between intelligent technologies and human expertise”.
The report highlights trends including AI Ethics and Cybersecurity 2.0, which help businesses balance innovation with governance, resilience and security.
As intelligent systems become increasingly embedded, robust safeguards and human oversight are becoming as important as the technologies themselves.
“Technology is transforming the way we work, but people remain the driving force behind every successful supply chain. The future of logistics will not be defined by
human versus AI
, but by how effectively organisations combine human expertise with increasingly capable technologies,” says Thomas Ogilvie, Chief Human Resources Officer and Labour Director at DHL Group.

title: Two Silverado EVs and a 150 kWh battery powered this entire concert tour
content:
Chevrolet
Chevy Silverado EV
Fred Lambert
| Sep 29 2026 - 8:01 am PT
Photo: © arbourphoto.com
A five-stop concert tour in Quebec ran entirely on two Chevrolet Silverado EVs and a 150 kWh mobile power plant this summer. No diesel generator, and no hookup to the grid.
I went to the final show, held in a grocery store parking lot in Montreal’s Saint-Henri neighborhood, and everything from the speakers to the stage lights to the kitchen was running off batteries.
A free tour powered by EV batteries
The tour, called “Le goût du paysage” (roughly “a taste of the landscape”), was put together by
Papillons
. That’s the Quebec company behind the RechargÉco fast-charging network, which it operates across Quebec and New Brunswick.
The idea was simple: bring Québécois artists Émile Proulx-Cloutier and Dumas, along with chef Oli cooking free corn dishes made with regional ingredients, to scenic spots across the province. Admission was free.
It ran from August 15 to 22 with stops in Trois-Pistoles, the Vallée Bras-du-Nord in Saint-Raymond, Parc Éco-Laurentides in Mont-Blanc, and Île-aux-Castors in Berthierville (that one sold out). The tour wrapped up with both artists on stage in the IGA parking lot in Saint-Henri.
Papillons billed the whole production as “100%” powered by EV batteries, with “zero emissions from start to finish.” Based on what I saw on site, that’s accurate.
One of the two Chevy Silverado EVs on the tour. Photo: © arbourphoto.com
Two pickups running the stage
The two Silverado EVs handled the stage: the sound system, the lighting, and the site lights once the sun went down. In Saint-Henri, I could follow the cable straight out of the power outlet in one truck’s bed to the stage.
A cable running from the Silverado EV’s bed outlet to the stage in Saint-Henri. Photo: Fred Lambert/Electrek
It’s a good job for the truck. The Silverado EV can be had with up to a 205 kWh battery pack, one of the biggest you can buy in a consumer vehicle, and GM rates its onboard power at 7.2 kW to 10.2 kW depending on the trim. We’ve already seen
GM run an entire mansion off a Silverado EV
when it launched its GM Energy products, and the
2026 Silverado EV
only pushed range further.
For comparison, Ford’s F-150 Lightning tops out at 9.6 kW of onboard power. And Tesla only just
added 2.4 kW of vehicle-to-load to the Model Y Premium
, and you need an $80 adapter for it.
Dumas on stage during the tour. Photo: © arbourphoto.com
The kitchen ran on a 150 kWh mobile power plant
The kitchen is the hard part. Cooking equipment pulls a lot of power, and it runs for hours.
For that, Papillons used a trailer-mounted mobile power plant with 150 kWh of energy capacity. It powered chef Oli’s kitchen at every stop.
Full disclosure:
my company,
, was involved in this project. We helped Papillons engineer the mobile power plant. Papillons isn’t ready to share more details about the system just yet, so I’ll leave it at that for now, but you can
reach out to them
if you are interested in such a product.
At the Saint-Henri stop, the trailer was parked right next to the kitchen tent, feeding full-size electric ranges topped with giant stockpots.
The trailer holding the 150 kWh mobile power plant, parked beside the kitchen tent in Saint-Henri. Photo: Fred Lambert/Electrek
The kitchen ran on electric ranges, all fed by the battery trailer. Photo: Fred Lambert/Electrek
Why bother with batteries in the city?
The show I attended was in the middle of Montreal. There’s power everywhere in Saint-Henri: the grocery store, the buildings around the lot, the streetlights.
The stage in the IGA parking lot in Saint-Henri, Montreal. Photo: Fred Lambert/Electrek
But having power nearby and being allowed to use it are two different things. Getting a temporary connection for an event usually means dealing with the utility or the property owner, hiring an electrician, and paying for all of it, often for a single evening. Plenty of organizers skip the headache and rent a diesel generator instead.
With batteries, you roll in, plug in, and you’re done. And on a stage where people are there for quiet acoustic songs, the lack of a rumbling generator behind the crowd matters.
But the real advantage showed up at the other four stops. A riverside island in Berthierville, a valley in Saint-Raymond, a park in the Laurentians. There’s no grid access at those spots, period. Normally, that’s where the diesel generators come out, if the show happens at all.
The Île-aux-Castors stop in Berthierville, with no grid power in sight. Photo: Papillons
And the energy itself is about as clean as it gets. The trucks and the power plant recharge on Quebec’s grid, which Hydro-Québec says is over 99% renewable, mostly hydro.
Electrek’s Take
Events are a great fit for mobile power supply. Festivals, outdoor concerts, film shoots, and construction sites burn a lot of diesel in rented generators, and they do it right next to people. A big battery on wheels does the same job silently, with no fumes, and it can be recharged at a charging station between stops. It helps that Papillons runs a fast-charging network.
The limit right now is output. Even the Silverado EV caps out around 10 kW per truck, which is plenty for sound and lights but not enough for everything.
But the concept works. I saw it work. It’s a great use case example for bidirectional charging, which I think is going to become an increasingly important part of the EV revolution.
